item.title: Marshall Guv'nor Genealogy (Part 1): The Story and the Circuit
item.description:
An original (circa-1989) magazine advertisement for the Guv'nor (planetbotch).

It’s a classic tale: they year is 1989, all the pros are using towering racks and amp stacks, and all you’ve got is a solid-state practice amp. Sure, it gets loud, but the gain channel just isn’t cutting it. You pop open the latest guitar mag and find a full-page advert for a pedal made by… Marshall? It even has an EQ section like a real Marshall amp (more on that later)! So you find one at a local shop, crank the gain, and finally coax some JCM800 from your Bandit.

The first celebrity player of the Guv’nor was Gary Moore. The back cover of his 1990 album Still Got the Blues features Gary playing his Les Paul through a Guv’nor pedal and into a Bluesbreaker-style combo. However, readers of this site will know the Guv’nor as Ed O’Brien’s primary distortion pedal throughout the 90s, providing mid-gain rhythm sounds for dozens of songs. Ed wasn’t far behind Gary, using his Guv’nor during the choruses of the 1992 single Creep.

Ed stomps on his Guv'nor during Radiohead’s performance of Anyone Can Play Guitar at the MTV Beach House on July 4, 1993. Given Ed’s love for pedals, it’s always fun to see his early setups, where a lone Guv'nor pedal is surrounded by preset controllers for rack effects.

The Guv’nor wasn’t Marshall’s first pedal (like many companies in the 60s, they sold re-branded Sola Sound fuzz and wah pedals), but it was their first in-house design, created by Steve Grindrod of vintage Marshall and 90s Vox fame. And even more notably, it was Marshall’s first pedal that attempted to capture the sound of their amps. In fact, it was probably the first pedal attempting to capture the sound of any specific amp (the original Sansamp was just a hair late, arriving in 1989).

The earliest dirt pedals in the 1960s were nearly all fuzz. By the late-1980s, there were plenty of overdrive and distortion pedals, designed to push an amp into higher gain. However, none brought the full controls of an amp to the floor, and none were voiced to emulate a particular amp. A Guv'nor advertisement from 1990 boldly proclaimed it “is more like a mini pre-amp than an ordinary distortion box.”* The profusion of “amp-in-a-box” pedals that we witness today is the legacy of the Guv’nor.

And that legacy isn’t just conceptual: a ton of popular pedals are direct clones or variations on the circuit of the Guvnor. It’s worth looking into the wide range of pedals that took inspiration from it — and not just because Jonny’s Shredmaster and Thom’s Bluesbreaker can both be considered variants! To do that, let’s first get an overview of the circuit. Then, in the next article, we’ll look through the variants themselves, using that circuit knowledge to understand what each variant brings to the table.

*By pre-amp, Marshall is referring to the the first stage of a guitar amp. The preamp usually contains the initial gain and tone controls. It’s followed by the power amp, which boosts the signal to a level (and converts it to an impedance) suitable for guitar speakers. In the 1980s, some guitarists with rack rigs would mix and match these elements. For example, Marshall sold separate tube preamp (model 9001) and power amp (model 9000) rack units.

Circuit Specifics

The easiest way to think about the Guv’nor’s circuit is to cut it in half. The first half hard clips the signal repeatedly, cutting bass and a bit of treble along the way. Then the second half provides adjustable tone-shaping with a three-band equalizer. The details of each half have a major impact on sound, as I’ll discuss in a moment, but this basic idea (multi-stage clipping followed by tone controls) will hold true for all of the Guv’nor’s variants and clones.

“Distortion” is a bit of a loaded term. In electronics, it refers to any alternation of a signal’s shape. But in the pedal world, “distortion” usually refers to hard clipping and “overdrive” to soft clipping (even though there are plenty of pedals that break those rules). So for this article, we’re sticking with the term “clipping” to describe the way a signal is boosted and squished.

A simplified block diagram of the Guv'nor. Less important for our discussion is the Guv'nor’s passive effects-loop, which even Marshall considered unnecessary and dispensed with in the otherwise identical (circuit-wise) Drivemaster. Intended to make the Guv'nor behave more like an extra amp channel, the effects-loop allows effects to be inserted after the distortion circuit, but before the bypass switch. Electrically it’s just a switched TRS jack, so it has no effect on the sound when not in use. It may seem convenient, but functionally it’s the same as putting the Guv'nor and other effects in a single bypass-loop, which is probably the reason few manufacturers have implemented the idea.

The Clipping Core

In 1991, Marshall discontinued the Guv’nor and introduced three new pedals: the Bluesbreaker, the Drivemaster, and the Shredmaster. All three pedals share a core circuit idea from the Guv’nor: clipping the input with a pair of opamp boosts, with a gain control that adjusts the boost of both stages simultaneously.

On most gain settings, the opamps are likely to hard-clip the signal, adding their own distortion. This is particularly notable in the Marshall pedals, as the TL072 opamps used have only moderate headroom, and are also susceptible to phase reversal when clipping (more info here).

The gain control also adjusts the tone of each stage. In the first, it cuts a bit of high-end as gain increases. In the second stage, gain cuts more bass as it’s turned up, reducing bloating at high gain. It’s a pretty clever arrangement. The idea to use single pot to control two opamp gain stages had previously appeared in Marshall’s solid-state amps, but none had this particular arrangement (and the amp version is arguably worse).

A schematic for the shared input section of the Guv'nor, Bluesbreaker, Drivemaster, and Shredmaster. We’re intentionally ignoring component values to keep the focus on structural similarities and differences between the pedals. Due to the buffered switching arrangement used, the original circuits technically had two caps and two resistors in series after the gain pot, but with a little math they can be safely simplified into just one resistor and one cap.

Diode Decisions

The two stages of opamp hard-clipping are followed by a pair of shunt diodes on the Guv’nor, Drivemaster, and Shredmaster. These diodes provide a third stage of clipping, and it’s one with a slightly softer knee than opamp clipping. The Shredmaster’s silicon diodes (1N4148) are the most extreme, squishing the signal down to just 20% of the range of the opamps. The Guv'nor’s and Drivemaster’s red Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) squish to a less intense 67% of the opamp’s range, and with a softer knee than the silicon (the knees are further aided by resistor choices, which help to magnify the difference). It’s been speculated that the choice of LEDs, which clip at a higher threshold and thereby provide a louder output, were chosen to compensate for the volume loss of the subsequent passive EQ stage on the Guv'nor and Drivemaster.

The Bluesbreaker is the exception, not just among the Marshall pedals, but among vintage overdrives in general. Instead of shunt diodes, it uses feedback diodes in the second stage, plus an extra “softening” resistor. Feedback diodes are the norm in vintage overdrives (just open up a Tubescreamer), but they’re usually found in non-inverting opamp circuits. That’s because feedback diodes usually hard clip in inverting opamp circuits. However, the single added series resistor makes a huge difference, causing the diodes to clip even more softly than in the more common non-inverting version. So instead of three hard clipping stages, it has two: one hard followed by one soft. Electrically, it’s an easy change (which is why many “royal” clones make it switchable), but it provides a dramatic difference in the character and feel of breakup.

The different dynamic response imparted by the multi-stage clipping arrangement is part of what makes the Bluesbreaker (and other Marshall pedals) so different from other popular overdrives like the Tubescreamer, which have only a single soft clipping stage. It’s far more impactful than the subtle differences in the choice of opamp type or the knee of any “magic” diodes. The other key differences are the tuning of the clipping filters and the choice of tone control, but we’ll leave those discussions for another day.

The Shaping Side

Now, let’s look a the second half of the circuit. On all four Marshall pedals, the clipping section is followed by adjustable tone shaping, and then finally a volume knob. It’s notable that none of these pedals provide any pre-gain adjustment, but it makes sense. Pre-gain tone controls are more disruptive; they can change not just the tone, but the feel and responsiveness of the clipping. Post-gain controls adjust the tonal balance, often to an extreme degree, but without fundamentally affecting the character of the clipping itself. Those familiar with Marshall’s amps won’t be surprised, since they also feature a tonestack at the very end of the preamp stage (more info here for the curious).

However, you might be surprised to learn that the Guv’nor’s 3-band EQ is a quite different design from the conventional Marshall tonestack. While the Guv'nor’s child the Shredmaster does feature a traditional Marshall tonestack (plus a totally unique Contour stage), the Guv’nor’s EQ is really its own thing. A look past the superficial similarities to the “FMV” (Fender/Marshall/Vox) tonestack reveals something more complex and more interactive. It features multiple added RC filters, some crossing between the controls, allowing for mid-forward and super-scooped sounds that are simply impossible with the FMV.

Once again, the Bluesbreaker is doing its own thing. Reflecting its more balanced tone, it keeps things simple with a single tone control that adjusts the intensity and frequency of two passive lowpass filters.

A graph showing the range of the “middle” control on a Guv’nor (green) a traditional Marshall (purple), with the “treble” and “bass” controls set at 10. Not only does the Guv'nor’s scoop extend twice as far, it also begins boosting the treble as the scoop increases! The traditional tonestack is less interactive, only subtly affecting the treble.

Sibling Rivalry

Although they share the same core, there’s far more difference between the Marshall pedals than you’d find between your average pair of overdrives. The three circuits each have a completely unique circuit for its adjustable tone shaping stage. This makes it impossible to get all of the sounds of one pedal using another. On our Oxford Drive, we added a “Voice” switch which, on the right Contour settings, does a good job capturing a neutral Guv'nor setting. However, there are extremes to each pedal that’re impossible to replicate without completely swapping out the EQ section.

Next week, we’ll take a look at the long list of famous pedals inspired by the Guv'nor, and you should now have the material to understand what makes each one unique (or a total ripoff, you be the judge).

A Little Extra: The Nitty Gritty

To understanding the structure of Guv'nor (and soon its variants), we’re ignoring the values of components that shape its various filters. But for those curious, here’s a frequency analysis of the first and second clipping stages of the Guv'nor. For this graph, each stage is isolated and simulated independently.

In the first stage (purple), the frequency of the bass shelving filter is fixed (723 Hz). The frequency of the treble filter decreases as gain increases, but it’s frequency is high enough that it’s only noticeable at high gain. Because the opamp hard clips in the first stage, these frequency changes effect the character of its distortion, and so they’re baked into the clipping of the stage.

In the second stage, the frequency of the lowpass filter is fixed (1064 Hz), while the frequency of the highpass filter increases as gain increases. Similarly, these frequency changes are baked in, affecting how the opamp in the second stage hard clips.

This combination of filters is only possible using multiple stages, and it’s largely responsible for the characteristic tone and of the Guv'nor. As such, you wouldn’t get the same sound by combining these two frequency responses into a single filter stage, then doing the clipping all at once.

item.title: Jonny’s Latest Electric Counterpoint Setup
item.description:
Jonny’s Latest Electric Counterpoint Setup

Jonny finger-picking during Reich’sElectric Counterpoint at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam on May 16, 2026 (33kbps).

Last week, Jonny performed Steve Reich’s Electric Counterpoint at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam. The concert also featured Jonny’s new Violin Concerto. Once again, he’s playing a sunburst Fender Telecaster. But although it displays a similar color to Jonny’s 90s favorites, the guitar differs in some significant ways. In fact, the guitar is quite new: it’s a Fender Player II Modified Telecaster!

This “Modified” variant of Fender’s Player II series was released only last year, and it’s primarily distinguished from the standard “Player II” due to the inclusion of Fender’s “Noiseless” pickups. The guitar is also set apart visually — both from the standard Player II and from the 1990s Plus — by its rosewood fingerboard and white Pearloid pickguard. The sticker on the upper horn is the produce label from a mango.

Jonny’s Telecaster is connected directly to a Boss FV50H volume pedal, which in turn connects to the vibrato channel of a Fender Twin Reverb amplifier. The “H” in the volume pedal’s name indicates that it’s the high impedance version, which provides a more consistent sweep when connected directly to a guitar’s output (the low impedance version is better suited for placement after buffers or with synths). That nothing is connected to the output of Jonny’s Petersen Strobostomp HD tuner, because it’s connected via the tuner output of the Boss FV50H.

Jonny’s setup for Electric Counterpoint at the Het Concertgebouw in Amsterdam on May 16, 2026 (anne.the.garbage.can).

When Jonny started performing Electric Counterpoint, he mentioned that he re-records the 12 backing guitar parts for each performance (he even once posted a Vine revealing the recording process). As at previous performances of the piece, the backing track is played back from Jonny’s laptop via an audio interface. In this case, it’s a Focusrite Scarlett Solo (Gen4). The interface connects to the concert hall’s sound system. Using an interface provides a balanced output, which is essential for avoiding noise when the signal is amplified to fill a hall.

There’s also an unused Strymon Brigadier delay pedal hidden underneath the amplifier. This is unusual, since Electric Counterpoint doesn’t require any effects (what many assume are loops or delays are in fact the aforementioned pre-recorded backing tracks). Perhaps Jonny was experimenting with the sound of delay in the hall during soundcheck, or perhaps he was testing it out as a source of ambience (in contrast to the more rhythmic delays he’s favored for the past decade).

Left: Jonny playing his new Fender Player II Modified Telecaster during the third movement “Fast” of Electric Counterpoint (karindeg). Note that he has the neck pickup selected.

Right: Jonny removing a headstock tuner from the guitar before the start of the piece (). Presumably he used it while warming up backstage (anne.the.garbage.can).

It’s worth looking a bit more into the new guitar. The instrument’s “Noiseless” pickups are designed by Fender to retain the sound of their traditional single coil pickups while mitigating the hum associated with them. In truth, they’re humbuckers, specifically an intentionally unbalanced form of stacked humbucker — the idea being that the upper coil reproduces the sound of the strings just like a regular single coil, while the lower coil is hidden and only attenuated the hum.

Tonally, the noiseless pickups are much brighter from the Lace Sensors in the Telecaster Plus V1 guitars that Jonny is known for. But spiritually, they’re quite similar. During the 90s, Lace Sensors were Fender’s hum-free option, offered on their modern-oriented guitars. It wasn’t until 1998 that Fender released their “noiseless” pickups, and stopped using Lace’s products (which is the reason modern pickups just say “Lace Sensor”, not “Fender Lace Sensor”). Then as now, Fender puts traditional single coil pickups in their vintage-inspired instruments. But the Telecaster Plus and Player II Modified are both guitars with features, like hum-free pickups, intended for modern players.

Jonny playing his American Professional II Tele during Electric Counterpoint at IRCAM on February 5, 2024. The amplifier is a Fender Tone Master Super Reverb (note the “Tone Master” medallion in the bottom right corner), a digital modeling amplifier with Jensen speakers (unknown).

In 2024, Jonny also used a recently released Fender Telecaster to perform Electric Counterpoint. That instrument was a Fender American Professional II Telecaster, and Jonny used it at the Hallé and at IRCAM. In terms of Fender’s lineup, the Professional II series is even more similar to the 1990s Plus series than the Player II series. It’s designed as the brand’s flagship modern Telecaster, with features like compensated saddles for better tuning, a push-pull switch for added tones, and 22 frets. It also sits in a similar place price-wise: pricier than the standard/player instruments, but cheaper than the more accurate vintage reissues and custom-shop editions. Of course, the Professional II’s vintage-voiced V-mod pickups definitely sound much brighter than the humbucker-voiced Lace Sensor Red and Blue pickups in a Plus V1. Clearly, Jonny is looking for those brighter tones, because he could just as easily have chosen an American Professional II Deluxe, which features Gibson-style humbuckers (for vintage-style Fender CuNiFe humbuckers, you’ll need to pay extra for the Vintage II Deluxe).

Hugh Brunt, who conducted the Violin Concerto, shared this after the concert (hugh.tieppo.brunt).

item.title: Hi Thanks for the amazing, inspirational site. Please keep it up. Any thoughts on why Jonny seems to have moved away from the EQD Pyramids flanger? It’s an amazing pedal (apart from the huge current draw!). Thanks again Frazer
item.description:
For live performance, Jonny tends to prefer pedals with simpler control layouts. If you look at his favorite phasor, tremolo, filter, freeze, and pitch pedals, they all have just two controls (I'm counting the Whammy's treadle as a control). The Earthquaker Devices Ghost Echo that he used for the last Radiohead tour also fits this trend, providing a more streamlined alternative to the Boss RV-5 pedals he used on the band's prior tour in 2018. Not only are these pedals faster to adjust between songs (or even by foot during songs), but they also lend themselves to Jonny’s style of stacking pedals to achieve distinctive sounds, rather than relying on all-in-one solutions.

Jonny’s pedalboard before the first show in London, on November 21, 2025 (thegigrig).

Jonny added the Pyramids to his setup during a time of peak pedal experimentation with The Smile. At that time, he tried other control-heavy pedals like the Strymon Timeline and EQD Organizer. Those were eventually replaced by more streamlined alternatives: the Boss DD-200 and Electro-Harmonix Pitchfork. He was also using new styles of pedals on his board. The flanger was one, but compressors, digital delays, and expression pedals were also new to his live boards. The Pyramids actually lasted a while, compared to the others he tried at first. It’s also worth noting that other pedals popped up in his setup during the 2023 recording sessions, but never made it onto his live board, such as the Electro-Harmonix Electric Mistress and Eventide H9.

The peak of experimentation: Jonny's pedalboard for The Smile's show in Anthem DC on November 23, 2022 (facebook).

By 2024, Jonny had streamline his guitar setup a bit. The Smile had just put out two albums in the span of a year, and so it seems the focus was on performing that material, rather than finding gear to write new songs. In part, it seems he’d found the types of pedals that worked for the band’s recent albums, but his attentions were also being pulled towards synths and cello. That said, he kept switching out pedals to keep things interesting. For example, he frequently had different compressor pedals on his primary and backup pedalboards. The same was true for his flangers. The Moog flanger he used most recently is notable not just for being more streamlined than the Pyramids, but also fully analog (the Pyramids is digital, which enables it to create so many different styles of flanging).

Jonny's backup board for The Smile's show in Hamburg on June 8, 2024. His main board for the show was similar, but featured a Moog flanger instead of the Boss.

You may be wondering: why devote so much attention to the question of a musician swapping out one pedal for another? We often get questions like this, and this seemed an educational example to explore. Ultimately, it has little to do with how “amazing” a pedal might be. For touring musicians, gear might be chosen solely for live shows — not just for easier adjustment on stage, but also because some things sound better at huge volumes and in highly reverberant venues. Jonny has spoken at length about the differences between recording and live performance, so it shouldn’t be a surprise that his gear might reflect this, even in a band as performance-focused as The Smile. One should also remember Jonny’s comment that “guitars are like typewriters. It's technology, it's not something to be admired or worshipped. Like, oh, a washing machine or something. It does the job."

item.title: Ranjha Updates and Backstory
item.description:
Ranjha Updates and Backstory

Jonny (Gibson ES-125), Shye (Vocal, Tanpura), Aamir (trumpet), Nafees (Qawwali Vocal), and Ehtisham (Dholak) playing Shemesh.

We’ve now updated Jonny’s pages to include details from the recent Ranjha and Shemesh music videos. These include updates to his Ebony Frost Tele Plus, Gibson ES-125, Hofner 182, Ampeg PF-50T, Fender Precision, and more.

Both songs are singles from the album Ranjha, a new collaboration between Jonny, Shye Ben Tzur, and the Rajasthan Express. The title is likely a reference a classical Punjabi folk tragedy. The Rajasthan Express themselves are an expansive group. Aamir Bhiyani primarily plays trumpet in Jazz-influenced wedding bands and parades, and doubled on euphonium and other brass for Ranjha. Zakir Ali Qawwal, Nafees Khan Ajmeri, and Ehtisham Khan Ajmeri are all from the Qawwali tradition, a form of harmonium-driven Sufi Islamic devotional music (the three have also performed together outside of this project). Nathulal Solanki plays Nagara, a large kettle-style drum which he describes as “loud and mostly played in temples”. He comes from a Hindu tradition, and said “we are all one group together, Hindus and Muslims… we are so proud that people know our music. And we are so happy” (indiewire).

Qawwali singers Zakir and Nafees singing on Ranjha. Zakir also plays harmonium. Zakir sings into a Beyerdynamic M88, while Nafees appears to sing into a Shure SM58. The small diaphragm condenser on the Harmonium is harder to identify.

Zakir Ali Qawwal previously sang with his brother, Zaki Ali Qawwal. Sadly, Zaki passed away on November 13, 2021. According to Shye, “[w]hile we were rehearsing, after a meal and a cigarette he departed on to another journey.”

The videos were filmed at Jonny’s home studio in Oxfordshire, which can be seen as a successor to Radiohead’s shared “Butts Furlong” studio (which was sold and converted to a home). Some details inherited from the Radiohead studio include the wooden podiums used for the headphone mixers and the large blue acoustic panels. The Smile’s albums Wall of Eyes and Cutouts were partially recorded at the studio.

The filming most likely took place in April or May of 2022. That was after the Smile’s first live shows at London’s Magazine, but before their first full tour that summer. As such, the photos give added insight into the gear that was likely favored during the recording of The Smile’s albums as well. For example, Jonny didn’t perform with his 1960s Hofner 182 until 2024, but we now know he was recording with it two years prior.

The API 2488 mixing desk at Jonny’s Oxfordshire studio (not Nigel’s API 2488), with an array of Sam Petts-Davies’s polaroids of members of the Rajasthan Express. The monitors are ProAc Studio 100 speakers.

(Left) Another angle of the same scene — this one shared to Sam Petts-Davies’s Instagram account on May 3, 2022. Sam engineered and mixed the sessions, and co-produced the album with Jonny. Junun was one of Sam’s first engineering credits, so its cool to see he’s taken an even greater role in its sequel.

(Right) Aamir Bhiyani, trumpeter of the Rajasthan Express, posted this selfie in front of Jonny’s API 2488 to his Instagram on April 29, 2022. It was part of a series of posts promoting (as you might guess from the caption) a show in London. Presumably, he used the trip to the UK as an opportunity to perform as well.

Aamir gives a cue while playing trumpet on Ranjha. The mic is a very rare Melodium 42B ribbon microphone, made in 1940s France (the recent 42Bn reissue looks similar, but lacks the brass ring on the mic’s mount). Jonny’s Hammond M102 organ can be seen behind him.

A closeup of Zakir playing harmonium on Ranjha.

A closeup of Nathu lal playing a pair of Nagara drums on Ranjha. The microphone is a (likely vintage) Neumann U47.

A shot of Ehtisham Khan Ajmeri playing a Dholak drum on Ranjha. The mic on the left head of the drum looks to be a Neumann U47, while the vocal mic looks like a Beyerdynamic M88 (this one with a grey grill, rather than the black grill on the one used by Zakir). The large shape behind him on the left is the open case of Jonny’s Tanpura.

item.title: Tour Highlights from ‘Hollywood Authentic’
item.description:
A photo of Thom reaching down to adjust the “Shift” knob on his Earthquaker Devices Hoof V2 fuzz (Greg Williams).

Last week, Greg Williams made a series of Instagram posts sharing photos from last November. The photos document Radiohead’s visit to Italy, with photos not only of their concert in Bologna but also the lead-up and aftermath. The photos were taken for a cover story in Williams’s magazine Hollywood Authentic.

Although the most surprising images are likely those taken backstage — such as Thom taking a nap post-yoga — the photos from soundcheck at the Unipol Arena provide some interesting gear details too. Though we’ve already covered most of this gear on our 2025 Tour Page, seeing things up close provide some new insights.

Thom’s Guitar Pedalboard

Though we’ve seen photos of Thom’s board on the recent tour (with all pedals listed here), it’s a rare treat to see individual settings!

Front and center is the Earthquaker Devices Hoof V2 fuzz. This pedal found its way onto Thom’s board during the Smile’s summer 2022 tour, and it stuck around for the rest of that band’s tours. Here, Thom is adjusting the Hoof’s “Shift” knob, which adjusts “mid content.” The Hoof is loosely based on the circuit of the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff, a pedal known for its huge, mid-scooped sound. The Shift knob makes the circuit more versatile by making those mids adjustable.

Thom’s Electro-Harmonix Holy Grail Nano reverb is blocked by his hand, but the settings on the Death By Audio Echo Dream 2 sitting beside it are clear. The Echo Dream 2 also made its way onto Thom’s board during the Smile era, and its chaotic sound is particularly associated with the single You Will Never Work In Television Again. Thom appears to have most of the knobs just shy of noon, giving a sound with equal amounts of fuzz and short, modulated delay.

The Strymon Timeline’s settings can be ignored, since they’re overridden by the currently selected preset, but it looks like that preset is titled “SLAPBACK” (a common term for a short echo with a single repeat). The Boss RE-20 Space Echo is set fairly atmospheric, but from the position of the mode switch it appears that the reverb is disabled (in spite of a label for the reverb level control).

The large, knobless pedal is actually used for Thom’s vocal microphone. It allows him to temporarily send the mic’s signal to a second signal path.

And perhaps the greatest mystery of all has been solved: the shape of the “STREAM/CENT” button and the extra text above it show that Thom is using a Boss TU-3 tuner, not a TU-2.

Jonny’s Modular Synths

As on Radiohead’s 2018 tour, Jonny brought two modular synthesizer racks. Each rack has the same set of modules made by Analogue Systems. On past tours, both racks were used for Idioteque, with one case serving as a backup for the other. On this tour, the rack on the left was configured differently for Sit Down. Stand Up. For more info on the modular, we have a full writeup (including modulargrid mockups) on Jonny’s page.

In the photo of Jonny’s modular, we can see the changes that Jonny made to his “drum machine” patch in order to play Sit Down. Stand Up. A notable difference is that he connected his sequencer’s TRIG 1 output directly to his RS-80 envelope generator to trigger a kick drum. This avoids the need for the RS-50 module, which he uses on Idioteque to convert the control voltages from the sequencer’s knob outputs into triggers of specified length.

We can also see that the TRIG 2 output is used to trigger Snare sounds, with a similar setup to Idioteque. And similarly, the TRIG 3 output (which outputs a trigger on every step) is connected to the clock divider. However, in contrast to Idioteque, the clock divider’s outputs are used to trigger hihats and beeping tones, rather than changing the pitch of the beeps. That’s because the beeps on Sit Down receive pitch CV from the top sequencer row, allowing Jonny to create more varied beeps and bloops.

Thom’s Nylon-String Guitar

Thom playing a classical guitar backstage. The exact instrument is unknown, but it’s different from the Taylor electro-acoustic classical that Thom used for the Smile’s performances in 2024. Perhaps this is the one used for the recording of The Smile’s Bodies Laughing (full analysis of that song here).

Colin’s Keyboards

A photo of Greg taking a photo of Thom with one of his Martin acoustics (Colin Greenwood via Greg Williams). In the foreground, we can see Colin’s two MIDI keyboards for the tour: a Roland PCR-500 (bottom) and an Arturia MiniLab 3 in black (top).

item.title: A Thirty-Year First: Jonny’s Stolen Ebony Frost Tele is Back
item.description:
Jonnying playing the stolen Tele during Ful Stop in Madrid on November 4, 2025 (Javi Dieguez).

When it came time to play Ful Stop last Tuesday, Jonny swapped his Honda-stickered Telecaster for one with no stickers at all. Swapping guitars for the song wasn’t new, since it requires a unique two-string capo, plus Jonny generally wears his guitar higher for the tune. But during the A Moon Shaped Pool era, Jonny usually played his “Uchuu Ace” Tele (his other guitar with a prominent 60s anime sticker on the pickguard) for Ful Stop. But in Madrid, he played an instrument with a more complex backstory.

This time, it was Jonny’s Ebony Frost Telecaster Plus, played at a Radiohead gig for the first time in thirty years (plus a month and two days). The guitar, which you’ve doubtless heard on the recording of My Iron Lung, was put in a van after Radiohead’s gig on October 2, 1995. The next day, it was stolen in Denver along with the rest of the band’s gear. Although we call the guitar his old “backup”, it was consistently used during the Bends era. He played it for nearly half the songs on the band’s famous Astoria gig.

Jonny playing the Ebony Frost Tele during Vegetable at the Astoria on May 27, 1994. Note the wear to the guitar’s upper horn.

After the theft, there was no sign of the guitar for almost 20 years. Then, in 2014, someone was browsing this very site and recognized the guitar as one they’d purchased in Denver during the 1990s. After we directed them to Radiohead’s guitar tech Plank, Jonny was reunited with the instrument.

Soon after, Jonny broke out the guitar for a couple of solo shows in Oxford and Geneva in February, 2015. But since then, it’s disappeared from view as Jonny’s love for Les Paul guitars deepened during his solo work on Junun and The Smile. This tour is the first time that Jonny’s playing it with Radiohead, once again using it as a “backup” for his main Tele.

Jonny playing the Ebony Frost Tele during the fourth Madrid show on November 8, 2025 (raphph).

item.title: Rhodes piano on Everything In Its Right Place
item.description:
From Everything In Its Right Place: Jonny sampling Thom’s voice with the Korg Kaoss Pad, Thom playing chords on the Rhodes (romeocrank).

Despite the fact that Nigel shared some incontrovertible evidence of Thom playing a vintage Prophet 5 on the recording of Everything In Its Right Place, it’s a common misconception that Thom played it on a Rhodes electric piano. But you can’t completely blame people for thinking it was the Rhodes, because Thom did perform the song on the vintage electric piano at Radiohead shows from 2001 to 2012.

However, for Radiohead’s shows from 2016-2018, the band switched to a new arrangement. Thom played the band’s Prophet ‘08 synthesizer, and the song’s outro was extended with a dance-y new bass-line from Colin.

This year, the band is back to the old arrangement! You can get a great view of Thom playing the Rhodes in this video. Perhaps Thom got all of his synth energies out in the past year, between his solo Everything tour and the release of his collaborative album Tall Tales with Mark Pritchard.

item.title: Ondomo on Present Tense

Ondomo on Present Tense

He switches back to tremolo picking on his Tele just before Thom returns to the refrain “in you I’m lost”.

Jonny taking a break from guitar during Present Tense to play some Ondomo (radioheadcommunity). Though the Ondomo is blocked by the Rhodes piano, we can see it on the screen above.

item.title: Jonny Greenwood’s Guitar Pedalboard for The Smile’s June 2024 Tour
item.description:
A photo of Jonny’s backup pedalboard in its flight case, from during the June 2024 tour.

Radiohead’s first tour in seven years begins today! We’ve already covered both Ed’s and Colin’s new boards for the upcoming tour (and we’ll have more info as the tour carries on). But we haven’t yet seen Jonny’s board, so we figured now would be a good time to share his most recent The Smile board. It’ll be interesting to see if his Radiohead board will be influenced by the pedals he tried with his newer band.

For The Smile’s initial shows, Jonny used the smaller of the two flight case style pedalboards that he’d previously used with Radiohead. However, for the fall 2022 tour, Thom and Jonny had matching custom wooden boards made for each of them. The boards are painted black, and feature risers for the back row of pedals.

Jonny had two of these custom boards for his guitar setup. They were kept nearly identical, allowing the crew to swap out the entire board if there was any issue. This was a lot easier than trying to troubleshoot the pedals and connections one-by-one as the entire audience waits, as they’d done in the past. However, there were always some small differences between the boards. Most often, it was a difference of a compressor, such as an MXR Dyna Comp on one board and a Telenordia Kompressor on the other.

Jonny also had separate, smaller boards for his bass guitar and cello. And that doesn’t include the Studiologic MP-117 MIDI pedals that he used to control various synths (initially an Oberheim SEM Pro module, later a Sequential Prophet 5 too), or the Blackstar Live Logic MIDI controllers used to trigger a Max patch that recorded and play back samples of Thom’s voice on A Hairdryer. Needless to say, there was a lot going on on the floor at those shows!

Jonny during The Smile’s show at Eventim Apollo on March 10, 2024 (Arend Kuester). Note that Jonny is already using the Moog Minifooger MF Flange pedal here. Also note the labelled outputs.

Main Signal Flow

Guitar ->

  • Peterson StroboStomp HD tuner
  • Origin Effects Cali76 Compact Deluxe
  • Electro-Harmonix Pitchfork pitch shifter
  • Earthquaker Devices Hizumitas fuzz
  • Moog Minifooger MF Flange (Backup: Boss BF-3 flanger)
  • Earthquaker Devices Astral Destiny reverb
  • Gamechanger Audio Plus sound sustainer
  • Earthquaker Devices Blumes overdrive
  • Boss DD-200 delay
  • Boss RE-202 Space Echo delay/reverb
  • Lehle P-Split III signal splitter

-> Fender ‘65 Reissue Super Reverb amplifier

Lehle Iso output -> 

  • Strymon Iridium amp modeler
  • Radial Engineering JDI Stereo direct box

-> FOH Mixer

All pedals are powered by a Strymon Zuma (top right) and Ojai (under the Astral Destiny).

The Nitty Gritty

The ToadWorks True-Bypass is used as a send/return for Jonny’s laptop audio interface (a Focusrite Clarett+ 8pre). This allows Jonny to process his signal with custom Cycling ‘74 Max/MSP patches running on his laptop. During the tour, he also used the his Max patches to process the sound of Thom’s vocal and of Robert Stillman’s clarinet and saxophone.

On early The Smile tours, as on Radiohead tours, Jonny brought a second amplifier as a backup. However, when he switched to the new custom pedalboards, he also started to use a Strymon Iridium as a backup amplifier. Presumably he’s using the Iridium’s “round” mode, a Fender Deluxe Reverb emulation, to capture the sound of his Fender '63 Reissue Super Reverb. To avoid ground loops and other issues, the Iridium is fed from the isolated output on a Lehle P-Split III.

Jonny generally has a direct box before his amp, which sends a copy of his signal to the FOH mixer. This functions both as a backup and as a way to get more mixing options. However, in this case the the Radial JDI Stereo is used to send both the left and right outputs of his Strymon Iridium to the mixer (note the “left” and “right” labels on his board in the Eventim Apollo photo).

In this shot of Jonny’s main board at a show in Prague’s Forum Karlin, we can just make out the Moog MF Flange pedal.

item.title: Colin’s 2025 Touring Pedalboard
item.description:
Radiohead’s upcoming tour is fast approaching, and preparations are well under way! Last week, Daniel Steinhardt from TheGigRig shared details of Colin’s new pedalboard! The board features all the classics, plus several cool additions! (Is that too many exclamation marks? It’s hard not to use them with all this exciting news!)

Read our full analysis with details and history on each pedal, or skip to the end for a list of everything…

Colin’s latest pedalboard! Photo shared by Daniel Steinhardton Sep 19.

Last month, we made a full analysis of Ed’s board for the upcoming tour. That board was shared on the main TheGigRig account, but Colin’s board was posted on Dan’s personal Instagram account. Dan seems to have really enjoyed building a board for Colin, saying:

“Amidst all the stress of running a business, looking after staff, planning, designing, imagineering, and the day to day grind, I do need to remind myself, I get to do some really cool stuff. Building this board has been so much fun and such an honour 🤓🙏”

Returning Giants

The mainstays of Colin’s pedalboard are back! Most prominent is the bright orange Lovetone Big Cheese. Acquired in circa-1999, it’s responsible for the fuzzy tone on live versions of The National Anthem, Packt like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box, and Myxomatosis. Partly hidden beneath the Cheese is Colin’s other fuzz pedal: the Shin-ei FY-2 he acquired in the mid-1990s. Colin uses its huge, scooped sound sparingly, saving it for a gut-punch at the end of Exit Music (for a film). Both fuzz pedals were part of Colin’s setup before he even had a pedalboard. Instead, they sat on top of his rack setup.

At the fore of the board is Colin’s SansAmp Programmable Bass Driver DI. He’s used the Sansamp since circa-2005, when he abandoned rack preamps and Gallien-Krueger heads in favor of Ampeg SVT heads. Colin uses the SansAmp for an overdriven tone on live performances of Ful Stop, and probably a few others too.

A big-box Electro-Harmonix Micro Synth appeared in a couple Radiohead gear photos over the years. It eventually landed on Colin’s touring pedalboard for the A Moon Shaped Pool era. This time, he’s using the more recent Electro-Harmonix Bass Micro Synth XO, which is a lot more micro than the original!

The Boss TU2 tuner is certainly less dramatic than the other returning favorites, but it makes up for that in its huge reputation as a standard on touring pedalboards. The paler orange color and the circular LEDs on the display show that it is indeed a TU2, not the more recent TU3. Colin has used a Boss tuner pedal since circa-2005, when he abandoned his massive Korg ToneWorks rack tuner.

A closeup of the SansAmp. Note the “FULSTOP” label under the LED for the SansAmp’s preset #1. Since the pedal uses presets, the knob positions can be ignored.

New Kids

Probably the most interesting new pedal on Colin’s board is an Origin Effects Bassrig ‘64. The Bassrig is an amp-in-a-box, replicating the circuit of vintage Fenders using transistors instead of tubes. It blends those with some bass-oriented features, like filters for the main output and a a dry blend control. It covers a lot of ground with Colin’s SansAmp, but perhaps the pedals cover different. Colin has the black panel version of the Bassrig, which is internally identical to the regular silver version.

The Origin Effects Cali76 Bass isn’t too much of a surprise—even Colin’s Boss-loving brother is using one of the boutique compressors on his The Smile board! And it makes sense: the Cali76 is based on the vintage UREI 1176 rack compressor that Nigel’s used countless times on Radiohead recordings. Colin’s Cali76 replaces the Diamond Compressor that he used during the A Moon Shaped Pool era. It’s a funny contrast with Ed, who went back to a Diamond after using a Cali76 on his Earth touring board. Like the Bassrig, Colin has the black panel version, which is internally identical to the regular silver version.

The Boss NS-2 Noise Suppressor might seem pretty innocuous, but it’s an a pretty interesting addition! Not only is it the first time Colin’s had a noise gate on his pedalboard, it’s the first time any member of Radiohead has had one! In the past, a noise gate was doubtless applied to Colin’s mic’d and DI signals at the FOH mixer. However, using a pedal reduces the noise at the source, meaning there’s less need to process all of the later signals as heavily. Removing the noise before Colin’s amp also means that there’s less noise on stage. However, it’s also possible that the NS-2 is only being used in combination with one particularly noisy pedal, perhaps the Shin-ei fuzz.

A closeup of Colin’s board, from a video shared by Dan, highlighting the QMX-2 switcher. Note patchbay on the right edge of the board.

True Bypass Switchers

Another new addition for Colin are true bypass loops. These keep the extra cables for each pedal out of the signal chain when not needed. They also just make it easier to turn pedals on and off. Each pedal gets a dedicated footswitch, in contrast to the controllers used by Ed (where each footswitch can be programmed to switch multiple loops simultaneously).

Colin is using a pair of TheGigRig’s Quartermaster bypass switchers. The one at the front of the board is a four-channel Quartermaster QMX-4. The smaller one, hidden under the riser, is a two-channel Quartermaster QMX-2.

A closeup of Colin’s board, from a video shared by Dan, highlighting the QMX-4 switcher. Note the individual labels for each effect.

More about the Board

All pedals are powered by a TheGigRig GENX14 DC power supply, which is mounted to the underside of the riser to keep it out of the way!

In a reply to his post, Dan also stated that the board itself is one of TheGigRig’s Large Single Tier boards.

Although most of the details of the board were shared on Dan’s personal page, one photo was stealthily shared on the main account too. The post only talks about the customizable rear panels on TheGigRig’s boards, but Colin’s Lovetone Meatball and the knobs of his Shin-ei Fuzz make it clear that this could be no one else’s board!

A photo of the back of Colin’s board, shared to the TheGigRig page on Sep 22. None of the pedals have a power cable connected, so this photo must’ve been taken partway through the build.

You might’ve noticed a stray, unplugged XLR cable in the other photos. It goes to the XLR connector on the back of the board. It’s a little surprising that the cable isn’t connected to the SansAmp, given how close together they are. But there’s also a couple of unplugged ¼" cables too. Perhaps the Radiohead crew are planning to stick a DI box in there?

The cables are all custom made for the build, each kept as short as possible. The right angle ¼" connectors are Eminence x TheGigRig Tiny Plugs. The straight ¼" connectors are Squareplug SPS connectors in black.

With the riser lifted up, we can see the GENX14 velcro’d to its underside (in the upper left corner of this image).

Pedal chain:

  • TheGigRig Patchbay
  • Boss TU2
  • Origin Effects Cali76 (QMX-4 #1)
  • Lovetone Big Cheese (QMX-4 #2)
  • Shin-ei FY-2 (QMX-4 #3)
  • Electro-Harmonix Bass Micro Synth (QMX-4 #4)
  • Boss NS-2
  • SansAmp Programmable Bass Driver DI (QMX-2 #2)
  • Origin Effects Bassrig '64 (QMX-2 #2)
  • TheGigRig Patchbay

item.title: Ed’s 2025 Touring Pedalboard
item.description:
On the most recent episode of GigRig’s ChatTGR series, Dan Steinhardt revealed the details of a new pedalboard setup for Ed. The segment on Radiohead is from 35:56-41:42, with video of a GigRig tech testing the board at 38:53-41:20. Dan also revealed that he’s building a board for Colin! However, Jonny doesn’t want a professionally made board, because Jonny “likes that his board doesn’t work, he likes that has to kick it.”

Dan has assembled Ed’s boards for a decade now, and often creates different ones not only for each of Ed’s projects, but also different ones for studio and touring. The new board is specifically designed for Radiohead’s upcoming European tour dates. Ed has spent a month with the new setup, and last Tuesday he met with Dan and expressed how happy he is with the new sounds he’s able to create with it.

Switching Systems

The new board consists of three distinct smaller boards. As Jake explains in the video, the left board is mainly overdrives, the center board is weird ambient effects, and the right board is delay effects.

Ed has used true bypass loops since the In Rainbows era, and he’s used TheGigRig switching systems since 2014 (before that he used Voodoo Labs switchers). These systems allows Ed to enable and disable any arrangement of his pedals by pressing a single switch on the controller unit. As Dan explains in the video, the G3S switcher on the primary board is the control center of the setup. It’s programmed with presets designed for specific songs. The G3S ATOM on each outer board is controlled by the central G3S. So the song presets on the center G3S apply to all three pedalboards.

Looking for New Sounds

Ed’s previous Radiohead touring board consisted of two boards, one with his core effects and one with weirder effects primarily used for newer songs. The core board featured a bunch of pedals aimed at creating the sounds of specific albums, such as a JHS Angry Charlie V2 (a modified clone of the Guvnor, used to recreate Ed’s 90s tones) and a ThorpyFX Muffroom Cloud (standing in for Ed’s Big Cheese fuzz).

This time, it looks like Ed is mainly using the newer effects he fell in love with while working on solo material. This applies to his drive board in particular, with a Kingley Harlot and Page at the core of his overdrive and distortion sounds. As such, it seems likely that older songs will take on a newer sound at the upcoming tour dates. In a sense, it may be reminiscent of Radiohead’s Haiti Benefit show. At that concert, Radiohead played songs from across their discography using only the gear they brought to LA to record The King of Limbs.

Full details of the new boards below. For a full description of all of Ed’s pedalboards since 1993, including all of Dan’s builds, check out this page.

Left Board: Overdrive and Compression

  • Xotic XW-1 wah
  • JHS NOTAKLÖN
  • Diamond Compressor (original version)
  • Kingsley Page V2 tube boost
  • Kingsley Harlot V3 tube overdrive
  • JHS Color Box V2 (10th Anniversary Edition)
  • TheGigRig G3S ATOM Switching System

Center Board: Pitch and Glitch

Top Row:

  • Sonic Research Turbo Tuner
  • Diamond Tremolo TRM-1 (Ed’s original in custom blue)
  • Hologram Electronics Microcosm
  • Hologram Electronics Chroma Console

Bottom Rows:

  • Gamechanger PLUS pedal
  • Gamechanger WET switch (PLUS pedal expander)
  • Electro-Harmonix Pitch Fork +
  • Digitech Whammy Ricochet
  • Red Panda Tensor
  • TheGigRig G3S Switching System

Floating (left of the center board):

  • unknown black pedal
  • unknown volume/expression pedal (maybe Dunlop DVP4 with some tape)

Right Board: Delay and Looping

  • Boss DD-3 delay (Ed’s original delay)
  • Boss DD-3T delay
  • OTO Machines BIM 12-bit delay
  • Electro-Harmonix Memory Man delay (vintage big box)
  • Line 6 DL4 MKII delay/looper
  • OBNE BL-44 Reverse
  • TheGigRig G3S ATOM Switching System

item.title: ‘Hamlet Hail to the Thief’ Rehearsal Gear
item.description:
Thom adjusts the modulation section on a Sequential Prophet-10 REV4 while keyboardist Tom Knowles plays and writer/arranger Justin Levine looks on. Photo by Manuel Harlan via NME.

Last September, Thom announced on Instagram that he’d adapted the music from Radiohead’s album Hail to the Thief to serve as the score to a new production of Shakespeare’s Hamlet. The project is a collaboration with directors Christine Jones and Steven Hoggett—Jones had previously worked with Radiohead as curator for the KID A MNESAIC game/exhibition. Thom described it as “an interesting and intimidating challenge .. !”

Earlier today, an article by Damian Jones on NME gave us the first glimpses at the new project! It’s encouraging to see that Thom is involved not only in the arrangement of the score, but also in the rehearsals! But perhaps that’s not too surprising, as it’s always exciting for arrangers to see how their written ideas are realized by the hands of live musicians.

Keyboards and Guitars

Before we dive into the details, here’s a quick highlight of the gear shown in the rehearsal photos:

  • Sequential Prophet-10 REV4 polysynth
  • Rhodes MK8 electric piano
  • Asaden Ondomo 100
  • Mellotron M4000D keyboard
  • Duesenberg Starplayer TV guitar in Vintage White
  • Rickenbacker 330 guitar in Ruby Red
  • Epiphone Casino guitar (?) in Cherry
  • Gibson ES-335 guitar in Sunburst
  • Fender Jazzmaster guitar in Black
  • Moollon P Classic bass in Lake Placid Blue

The keyboards are all reliable modern version of vintage instruments. It’s unknown how much (if anything) is loaned from Radiohead, and how much was purchased or rented for the production. The guitars all appear to belong to the guitarists, however.

Asaden Ondomo 100

By far the biggest surprise in the rehearsal photos is the presence of an Ondomo!! Released in 2016, the Ondomo is a modern replica of the rare, vintage ondes Martenot. Jonny’s 1980s ondes Martenot and his French Connection (a Martenot-inspired CV-controller comissioned by Jonny) are all over the recording of Hail to the Thief. In fact, Where I End and You Begin features the instrument so heavily that Jonny dedicated it to Jeanne Loriod, who died tragically in 2001. Loriod was the world’s leading exponent of the Martenot, and along with her sister Yvonne, was the primary interpreter of Messiaen’s Turangalîla-Symphonie. Jonny also interviewed Jeanne shortly before her death.

The ondes can also be heard on 2+2=5, Myxomatosis, We Suck Young Blood, and Scatterbrain. The Martenot section on Jonny’s page features a list (with timestamps) of every Radiohead song that includes the Martenot.

Jonny with his Ondomo during a soundcheck or performance of Desert Island Disk.

Each of the 100 original Ondomo were handcrafted by Naoyuki Omo with the help of the Japanese Radiohead Tribute Band OAS. As such, each is unique. Jonny has used four different Ondomo on Radiohead tours since 2017, all with unique customizations for Jonny. His original was returned to OAS, and we documented it extensively in this post.

The Ondomo in the rehearsal photos is in natural finish, which was the most common, with a brown grill-cloth. It features a later version of the “drawer” (“tiroir” in French), which holds the “touche” volume key and timbre controls. It also appears to be missing its travel handle. It bears some resemblance to the Ondomo that Jonny used for an earthquake benefit concert in Fermo, Italy in 2019.

Prophet-10

The header photo from the article shows Thom once again tweaking a Prophet synthesizer. This time it’s a Prophet-10 REV4. It seemed as though Thom and Jonny preferred the more historic restriction of only five voices, as they’d instead used the Prophet-5 REV4 for the recent The Smile and Everything tours. But perhaps this productions requires some richer chords. Our article on the Everything tour also includes a photo of Thom adjusting the modulation section of the Prophet.

A screenshot of Thom playing his 1963 Fender Jazzmaster during the first “performance” of There There on Radiohead’s Amateur Night II webcast on Feb 10, 2000. On the left, one can see the band’s original vintage Prophet 5 resting on top of their vintage Rhodes piano.

Rhodes Piano

Beneath the Prophet is a Rhodes Mk8 electric piano, standing in for Radiohead’s beloved 1970s Rhodes Mk1 Suitcase electric pianos. Released in 2021, the Mk8 hearkens “back to the classic, warmer Fender Rhodes sound from the early ’70s” , with mechanical parts that’re “far superior quality to the original”, but carrying “a high price tag.” The Mk8 in the rehearsal photo is customized with a black hood and a walnut bottom shell. Although we only have a one minute clip from the recording of Hail to the Thief, the logo of a Rhodes Mk1 Suitcase is prominently visible. Hail to the Thief ultimately features much more acoustic piano than electric, so perhaps Thom’s rearrangements call for additional Rhodes sounds.

A screenshot of Radiohead recording 2+2=5 at Ocean Way Studio B in September, 2002. Radiohead’s Rhodes piano and Crumar string synthesizer can be seen on the bottom right (youtube).

Mellotron

Radiohead first purchased an original Mellotron M400 during the recording of OK Computer. The band bought it on Jonny’s initiative, and it’s in fact the very same one used by Tangerine Dream in the 1970s. That vintage M400 has appeared every so often in studio photos, but for touring Jonny and his keyboard techs sampled their Mellotron onto an Akai S3000XL sampler, then later a laptop running Native Instruments Kontakt.

The Mellotron M4000D seen in the rehearsal photos is digital reissue (hence the “D”) . It was released in 2007 by Streetly Electronics, the same company who’d made M400 in the 1970s. The M4000D is essentially a high quality sampler with a similar control interface (wooden keybed, knob layout) as the original. A “mini” version with a smaller cabinet was released a few years ago, but the one seen in the rehearsal photos is the full-size version.

The edge of a Strymon BigSky Reverb can be on the floor beside beneath the Mellotron.

Vocalists Ed Begley and Megan Hill. Photo by Manuel Harlan via NME. The small box on a stand in front of each of vocalist if a Allen&Heath ME-1 40-channel headphone mixer. The other musicians are using the same ones. The Asaden Ondomo 100 and Mellotron M4000D can be seen on the left.

Vocal Setup

The vocalists are using a wireless microphone setup, presumably to give them the flexibility to move around during the play. The system combines elements from a few different brands. The wireless microphones combine Sennheiser’s SKM 6000 body with DPA SE2-ew capsules. And for receivers, they’re using Sure P10R+ bodypacks. Hopefully future photos will reveal what effects the mics will run through—perhaps a FOH setup similar to the one for Thom’s solo Everything tour.

Guitars and Bass

A glance at the Instagram accounts of the guitarists shows that the guitars belong to them, including the Rickenbacker 330 in a rare Ruby Red finish belonging to Adam Martin. The black Fender Jazzmaster does look similar to Thom’s No3, but it has a maple fingerboard in contrast to the rosewood on Thom’s guitar.

Guitarists Jenny Clifford and Adam Martin, and bassist Joe Downard. Photo by Manuel Harlan via NME.

item.title: Thom’s Acoustic Guitars at the Horseshoe Tavern
item.description:
“Some bloke from some band” on March 28, 1995.

Yesterday was the 30th anniversary of the release of The Bends! To commemorate the occasion, Radiohead dug up a VHS tape recording of Thom performing an acoustic set at Toronto’s Horseshoe Tavern on March 28, 1995. It’s hard not to get emotional seeing such an early acoustic performance of (nice dream), after Thom played it acoustic for the first time in over a decade during his solo tour last November (he used a Martin 00-18 for that show). The contrast between the raw nerves of the early performance and the relaxed confidence of the recent is quite striking.

For the Horseshoe Tavern show, Thom alternated between a 6-string guitar and a 12-string guitar. The 6-string isn’t surprise, as Thom played a ton of acoustic on songs in the 90s. Lately, it’s been pretty rare to see Thom use a 12-string (his Zermatt performance of These Are My Twisted Words a couple years ago was a pleasant surprise). But in the mid-1990s, Thom brought out a 12-string for acoustic gigs and televised performances on a quite a few occasions.

Takamine EN10C

The 6-string acoustic is a Takamine EN10C. It was Thom’s primary touring acoustic when promoting The Bends in 1994 and 1995. Thom switched to a Takamine EF261SAN in 1996, likely as a result of the theft of the band’s gear in Denver in late-1995. Thom perhaps most notably used the guitar to play Fake Plastic Trees on Late Night with Conan O’ Brien on June 12, 1995. By that Thom, it featured Apple and Astroboy stickers, as was common for Thom’s guitars at the time. In can be seen in footage both of other live shows and of other TV performances. The guitar was also borrowed by Jonny for some acoustic shows, which provide the best quality footage of the instrument. Thom always used a tan-colored guitar strap with the acoustic.

Two shots of Thom with the EN10c during the Horseshoe Tavern gig. The footage is pretty oversaturated, making the guitar appear reddish. One can just barely see the tan guitar strap.

Thom with his Takamine EN10C on during High and Dry on Later… with Jools Holland on May 16, 1995 (radiohead.com).

Alvarez DY87-12V

The 12-string acoustic is an Alvarez DY87-12V. Thom used the exact same guitar for other acoustic performances (nice dream), Street Spirit (Fade Out), and Bulletproof… I Wish I Was during the same era (note the same “Fender” guitar strap). The “Alvarez” logo on the guitar’s headstock can be seen more clearly in the Street Spirit video. Guitars made by Japanese maker K.Yairi were rebranded Alvarez when sold in certain regions (mainly the USA and Japan), so it’s likely that Thom acquired the guitar on tour. For more info on the brands, and on Thom’s YD-88 acoustic that he favored during the OK Computer era, check out this post.

Two shots of Thom with the EN10c during the Horseshoe Tavern gig. Even in the oversaturated footage, one can distinguish the guitar’s sunburst finish, larger headstock, and Fender-branded guitar strap.

The EN10c wasn’t the only guitar stolen from the band in Denver on October 3, 1995. All of the band’s touring guitars were taken, many of them the same instruments in studio for Pablo Honey and The Bends. For a clearer picture of the stolen gear that formed the foundation for The Bends, check out our full rundown of the band’s rig for their 1994 performance at London’s Astoria. The band were so proud of that gig, they even used the live recording of My Iron Lung (with some overdubs) for the album release.

item.description:
Thank you very much for the submission!

This photo is doubtless from a performance of Motion Picture Soundtrack. During 2000 and 2001, Thom experimented with various digital organ keyboards for performances of the song. He paired the organs with an Electro-Harmonix Micro Synthesizer effects pedal in order to get a more distorted sound, presumably to better emulate the crunchiness of the late-1800s Putnam & Co pump organ/harmonium used on the original recording. Colin likely played the same double bass as in the photo, a South Korean student model bass, for the studio recording of the song. However, the harps on the studio recordings are samples which Jonny processed. The choir near the end is also a sample, specifically one from the 1963 film Donovan's Reef (this was identified by casiopeia67).

Jonny sitting at the band's Putnam and Co pedal organ at Radiohead's studio during the recording of In Rainbows in 2006-2007. It's worth noting that this is the same instrument that the band used for Thinking About You on Pablo Honey (listen at the very end of the song to hear the same mechanical noises from the organ as during Motion Picture Soundtrack). The band purchased it from Chipping Norton when that studio closed down in 1999.

The particular digital organ visible here is a Korg CX-3 — specifically the version produced from 1979-1991. The later digital version, produced from 2001-2011, has the "CX-3" model number printed on the back panel next to the "Korg" logo. At a glance, the CX-3 looks very similar to Jonny’s Hammond XB-2. Both have a single manual of 61 waterfall-style keys, both have wooden cabinets, and both have a set of drawbars in a control panel to the left of the keyboard. These similarities are unsurprising, as both are “clone-wheels”: replicas of Hammond tone-wheel organs meant to be more portable than a vintage B3. But perhaps the most notable difference between the keyboards is that the original CX-3 used analog technology, while both the later CX-3 and the Hammond XB-2 used a digital sound engine.

Thom playing an organ during Motion Picture Soundtrack in Toronto in 2000. Note the EHX Micro-Synthesizer pedal on top of the pedal. In addition to it, there is also a direct box and what appears to be a small speaker (presumably serving as a monitor).

In fact, although we’ve written that Thom borrowed the XB-2 for performances in 2000, it’s possible that he in fact used the CX-3. The keyboards are extremely similar in a side-profile, particularly in the blurry footage we have of the band’s show in Toronto on October 17, 2000. The 2000 tour seems to be one of their worst-documented, so hopefully someone can dig up some more photos or footage.

Here are a couple photos of the control panels of an original Korg CX-3 (left) and a Hammond XB-2 (right) (Audiofanzine: CX-3, XB-2). The similar placement of the drawbars and buttons makes the keyboards hard to distinguish. However, the XB-2 has an additional panel beneath the keyboard with buttons and a small LCD display (these extra buttons control a variety of features, from vibrato tuning to preset selection). In contrast, the Korg has an overall thicker wooden cabinet. The newer version of the CX-3 has an added panel above keyboard for the drawbars, which makes it easy to distinguish.

Jonny playing his Hammond XB-2 during Nude (then called Big Ideas) at a soundcheck on April 17, 1998 at the Radio City Music Hall in New York (source: Meeting People is Easy).

item.title: The MIDI Control Center of Thom’s 2024 Solo Tour
item.description:
Thom adjusts a knob on his Prophet 5 REV4 during a show in Auckland, New Zealand (Azrie).

The core of Thom’s electronic setup for his 2024 solo tour is a K&M keyboard stand holding up a Sequential Circuits Prophet 5 REV4 and a mysterious box with angled wooden side panels. The mysterious box is a rack case containing two units: an Elektron Analog Rytm MK2 drum machine and a Sequentix Cirklon MIDI and CV/gate sequencer. The Rytm is mounted in the case using RMK-3b rack ears.

Sequential Prophet 5 REV4

Thom’s been a fan a Prophet 5 since the late-90s. But at the time, the only Prophet 5s available were from the late-70s and early-80s, and they were becoming too delicate to tour with (heck, many found the REV2 to be too delicate at the time of release, hence the switch from SSM to Curtis filter chips). Though Thom brought a Dave Smith Prophet 08 and later a Sequential Prophet 6 on tour during the 2010s, it wasn’t until the reissue of the Prophet 5 in 2020 (dubbed “REV4”) that Thom started touring with one. The Smile have brought a Prophet 5 REV4 on tour since 2022, though it’s mainly played by Jonny.

So far this tour, Thom has used the Prophet 5 for quite a few songs, including All I Need, Kid A, Cymbal Rush, Hearing Damage, and Truth Ray.

In a clip by @hamishtimmins from a show in Auckland, we can see Thom adjusting the depth of the envelope modulation in the Poly-Mod section of the Prophet 5 during Everything In Its Right Place. Near the end of the clip, we can also see him adjusting a knob on his Prophet 6, so it’s clear he’s layering Prophets to get that enveloping sound. Also note the Intellijel sticker on the back of the Prophet 5 — Thom had the same one on his phone case in 2022.

Elektron Analog Rytm MK2

As for the Elektron Analog Rytm drum machine, this is the first time we’ve seen Thom with a MK2. However, he was a big fan of the Analog Rytm MK1 around the time of its release in January 2014. Thom could be seen with the Rytm at the earliest shows in support of Tomorrow’s Modern Boxes (released September 2014), making it likely that he used the Rytm (along with his Elektron Analog Four) for the recording of that album. The Rytm MK1 remained a core of his setup for solo tours in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2019. He was unusually candid about the machine in a 2019 interview with Elektron, saying “I use it a lot live because it’s so quick and it sounds really huge.” The Rytm probably saw some use on the recording of ANIMA as well, but Thom highlighted the Octatrack in particular for use on that album.

Thom can be seen tweaking the Rytm in this video by Elly of Packt Like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box in Auckland.

In this photo by Ben Dickens from the show in Auckland on October 25, we can see the connections on Thom’s Analog Rytm MK2. All of the MIDI jacks are wired up, showing that the Rytm is both controlled by other gear (probably receiving clock and pattern changes from the Cirklon) and controlling other gear (probably sending MIDI sequences to synths). All eight of the individual track outputs are wired up. Interestingly, he’s also using the “left” main output, presumably for the remaining four drum tracks (tracks can be individually routed to the main output, so it can be used as a ninth individual out if desired). He isn’t using the extra “control” inputs or the “external” inputs. However, he is using the left “audio” input, which means he’s likely doing some live sampling! More info the Rytm’s connections can be found on page 12 of the unit’s manual.

Though mainly marketed as a drum machine, on account of its internal analog drum synthesis, the Analog Rytm is also a powerful sampler and MIDI sequencer. So it’s likely controlling other bits of gear as well. That said, it appears that Thom’s main sequencer is a little more esoteric…

Sequentix Cirklon

The Sequentix Cirklon is a dedicated hardware sequencer. Though it creates no sounds on its own, it offers a huge range of options to control other gear, including up to 64 tracks. In addition to five dedicated MIDI I/O ports, the Cirklon also offers a multi-channel bus of CV/gate outputs. With a wide range of behaviors (how it moves through steps) and options for randomization, it’s designed to make even simple MIDI patterns feel more alive and dynamic.

Thom can be seen adjusting both the Analog Rytm MK2 and the Cirklon during this video by Lori Shmori of Atoms for Peace. In fact, it appears the Cirklon is both controlling the synth bass and triggering some sounds on the Rytm, while the main beat is programmed on the Rytm’s own sequencer. It’s interesting to hear which elements of the beat Thom has adjusted over the years, compared to what he played on his Rytm (MK1) at Pathway to Paris in 2015.

We’ll have more on the rest of Thom’s setup in the coming week…

item.title: Sam Petts-Davies’s Setup for Thom’s ‘Everything’ Tour
item.description:
A photo of the setup, shared by Sam on his instagram account with the caption “tour begins tonight. i’ll be parked at front of house with this box of esoterics for the duration. it’s going to be something really special.”

Thom’s solo tour has just begun with a show in Christchurch, New Zealand, and Sam Petts-Davies is along for the ride!

Since Radiohead’s earliest shows, there’s always been at least a few effects added by an engineer at the FOH (front of house) mixing desk to keep the band’s sound clear and coherent. With Radiohead, that role was filed by Jim Warren. Even after Thom started bringing pedalboard full of vocal effects on tour, Jim continued to apply additional effects including plugins such as the Waves C4 multiband compressor for vocals. You can find more info on Jim’s work in these posts.

For The Smile, even fewer hardware effects were needed at the FOH desk, in part due to Thom’s expanded vocal pedalboard. In 2022, the Smile’s mix engineer mainly relied on plugins from an Avid VENUE S6L-32D digital desk, supplemented only by a TUBE-TECH CL 1B Tube Optical compressor (presumably for Thom’s vocals).

It’s clear that when Thom is performing totally solo, a different approach is needed. But it’s hard to imagine that any past FOH setup has been so full of hardware effects! And not just effects, but also modulators and an usual mixer, as we’ll see….

For those who don’t know, Sam initially served as a engineer under Nigel during the recording of Junun in 2015. He subsequently did engineering work on Spectre, A Moon Shaped Pool, and on the strings for the OKNOTOK singles. In 2018, he co-produced the soundtrack to Suspiria with Thom, and apparently Thom was a fan because Sam received a full production credit for Thom’s soundtrack to Confidenza. He also produced both of the Smile albums released this year: Wall of Eyes and Cutouts.

For comprehensibility, we’ve divided the setup into four sections: the core, the modular, the pedals, and the rack. We’ll start with the core setup.

Core Setup

This section is the nexus: receiving input from Thom’s stage setup, sending it through various effects, and mixing it all together. The Matrix Mixer is using to both mix together and feedback the various effects in Thom’s eurorack setup. The Yamaha DM3-D appears to be the central mixing console for the entire setup. Despite its small size, the Yamaha boasts 22 channels and a huge range of built-in effects, and on top of that it can also run VST plugins.

  1. Death By Audio Echo Master delay
  2. ? Electro-Harmonix 45000 looper
  3. Roland RE-201 Space Echo tape delay
  4. ?
  5. Erica Synths Matrix Mixer
  6. Yamaha DM3-D Digital Mixing Console

Modular Setup

In the decade since Thom first used a Make Noise Shared System Plus to process his voice and piano, his eurorack effects setup has expanded quite a bit! The Shared System is designed to be both a sound generator and an effects processor, and since then Thom has created dedicated setups for each of those applications. This setup is the effects processor, with lots of delays, filters, and reverbs, plus some LFOs and CV sources to modulate those effects. The additional Doepfer case that Thom has on stage, might have some of his sound generators, but knowing Thom it could just as easily be even more Make Noise Echophon delays.

Row 1 (left to right):

  • Make Noise Maths (unused)
  • Intellijel Planar² joystick
  • Xaoc Devices Belgrad dual filter (unused)
  • 4ms Dual Looping Delay
  • 4ms SISM: Shifting Inverting Signal Mingler
  • blank panel (4hp)

Row 2 (left to right):

  • 4ms QCD: Quad Clock Distributor (unused)
  • Soma Lyra8-FX (unused)
  • Make Noise Echophon delay
  • Make Noise Erbe-Verbe reverb
  • Vermona TAI-4 transformer-isolated I/O

Row 3 (left to right):

  • Intellijel µMIDI interface
  • Make Noise Richter Wogglebug random generator
  • Make Noise MULT
  • Make Noise QPAS dual filter
  • Rossum Electro-Music Panharmonium spectral resynthesizer
  • ? Make Noise Memophon delay
  • Vermona TAI-4 transformer-isolated I/O

Row 4 (left to right):

  • Make Noise Morphagene sampler
  • Mannequins Three Sisters filter
  • Mannequins Just Friends
  • Qu-Bit Aurora reverb
  • Earthquaker Devices Afterneath reverb
  • unknown module (2hp)
  • Xaoc Devices Kamieniec phaser

It appears that these are Thom’s Rows 1 and 2 are kept in a Doepfer A-100P6 Suitcase 6U case. Rows 3 and 4 are kept in a Doepfer A-100PB Suitcase Base case. The modules on row 4 are impossible to identify at this angle, but Make Noise style knobs are clearly visible on the left-most module.

Pedal Setup

  1. Furman M-8Lx power supply
  2. ? Radial Engineering EXTC-Stereo reamp
  3. Eventide Pitchfactor
  4. ? Hologram Chroma Console
  5. Empress Effects Reverb

Rack Setup
